summary: Defines MIB objects that allow configuring middleboxes, such as firewalls and network address translators, so communication can pass through them. The objects follow closely the MIDCOM semantics of RFC 5189. It is a standards-track specification.

plainLanguage.summary: This is a settings sheet for firewalls and address-translating boxes, written in the shared format network tools can read and change.

how does midcom work over snmp
what is a midcom policy rule
how to secure midcom mib access
subtitle: An SNMP MIB that lets applications ask firewalls and NATs to open pinholes and create address bindings.

tldr.problem: Firewalls and NATs obstruct applications that use dynamically negotiated UDP or TCP ports, and the MIDCOM semantics of RFC 5189 needed a concrete way to talk to such middleboxes.
tldr.mechanism: The MIDCOM-MIB maps MIDCOM sessions and transactions onto SNMP: policy rules are rows in a table that a client creates and enables, replies come back as SNMP notifications or by polling, and SNMPv3 handles authentication and access control.
tldr.outcome: A MIDCOM client can request firewall pinholes and NAT bindings and monitor the resources used, as long as the middlebox is secured with SNMPv3 and strict access control.

today: RFC 5190 is a Proposed Standard, and the metadata records no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It follows the MIDCOM semantics of RFC 5189.

sections.title: Controlling Middleboxes with a MIB
sections.content:
This memo defines a portion of the Management Information Base (MIB) for controlling firewalls and Network Address Translators (NATs). Both belong to the group of middleboxes: devices on the datagram path between source and destination that do more than IP routing. They can obstruct packet streams, for example when dynamically negotiated UDP or TCP port numbers are used, as in many peer-to-peer applications.

The IETF MIDCOM working group defined a framework (RFC 3303), requirements (RFC 3304) and protocol semantics (RFC 5189) for communication between applications and middleboxes. In that model a trusted third party, the MIDCOM agent, assists the middlebox without the middlebox needing application intelligence. The MIB lets applications request pinholes at firewalls and address bindings at NATs, and also reports the resources those requests use.

The RFC replaces the term MIDCOM agent with MIDCOM client, because in SNMP the agent is the server side. The MIDCOM client is the SNMP manager, and the middlebox is the SNMP agent.
sections.plainLanguage: Some doors in a network only open if someone asks nicely. This document defines the form for asking, using a format that network tools already know.

sections.title: Mapping MIDCOM Sessions onto SNMP
sections.content:
SNMP has no sessions: its context lasts for a single request and reply. The MIDCOM-MIB therefore models a session in a very static way. Authentication and access control happen on every message, using an SNMPv3 security model such as the User-based Security Model (USM, RFC 3414) and the View-based Access Control Model (VACM, RFC 3415). The only dynamic part is that a client can switch on and off the notifications the middlebox sends, using the SNMP-NOTIFICATION-MIB. For this reason Asynchronous Session Termination is not modeled.

The RFC notes that per-message security can be seen as overhead compared with per-session security, but it meets the security requirements of middlebox communication.

Access control may also be driven by an access control policy system. The SNMP agent then acts as a policy enforcement point, and the policies must be turned into configuration such as VACM. Rules owned by user A can, for example, be hidden from user B, readable by user C and modifiable by user D. Restrictions such as allowing requests only for certain IP address ranges may need to be enforced by the MIB implementation itself.
sections.plainLanguage: SNMP forgets you after every message, so instead of a long visit, you show your ID each time you knock.

sections.title: Transactions over SNMP Operations
sections.content:
MIDCOM transactions do not map one-to-one onto SNMP, so the RFC maps each kind separately.

  • Asynchronous transactions become SNMP notifications whose parameters are managed objects. Notifications usually travel as unreliable UDP packets, so a client expecting one may need to poll.
  • Configuration requests are written with one or more SNMP SET transactions, because a request may not fit in one UDP packet. Completion of the last SET tells the middlebox to start processing.
  • Configuration replies come either as an SNMP notification followed by optional GET transactions, or by the manager polling with GET until processing ends. Polling takes more operations but is more reliable.
  • Monitoring transactions are a sequence of SNMP GET transactions.

Atomicity is therefore not fully guaranteed. Monitoring, Policy Reserve Rule and Policy Enable Rule transactions may span several operations, so items can change in between. The middlebox sends notifications about such changes, and the client can repeat the transaction or merge the notifications into its result. All of these problems can be avoided by sending all request parameters in a single SET. Lifetime change transactions stay atomic, and to avoid idempotency problems from a retransmitted SET it is RECOMMENDED to include snmpSetSerialNo or keep the retransmission timer below the smallest requested lifetime.
sections.plainLanguage: A big request is like a long letter sent in several envelopes, and the box only starts working when the last envelope arrives. The answer comes back as a ping, or you can keep asking if it is ready.

sections.title: Structure of the MIB Module
sections.content:
The module has three kinds of managed objects: transaction objects, configuration objects (the capability information is mandatory) and optional monitoring objects.

The central table is midcomRuleTable, with one row per policy rule, whether it is being established, failed, established or terminated. Rows are indexed by midcomRuleOwner, midcomGroupIndex and midcomRuleIndex, and are created by writing midcomRuleRowStatus. A client first writes the request parameters, then writes reserve(1) or enable(2) to midcomRuleAdminStatus to start processing. midcomRuleOperStatus shows the current state. A row is removed when both midcomRuleLifetime and midcomRuleStorageTime count down to 0, or the client sets both to 0. Other objects cover the interface, flow direction, transport protocol, port range and midcomRuleMaxIdleTime.

The rule also carries address tuples A0 (internal endpoint), A1 (middlebox inside address), A2 (middlebox outside address) and A3 (external endpoint). The client must specify A0 and A3, which can be a problem for applications that are not firewall-friendly, such as FTP using the PORT command instead of PASV, when the middlebox offers twice-NAT.

midcomGroupTable entries are created automatically when rules use a group index, and removed with the last member. Writing midcomGroupLifetime changes the lifetime of all member rules, so groups give a shortcut for handling, say, all rules of one application session.
sections.plainLanguage: Each request is one line on a clipboard. You fill in the line, then tick the box that says go, and lines with the same group label can be handled together.

sections.title: Configuration, Monitoring and Notifications
sections.content:
Capabilities. midcomConfigMaxLifetime gives the longest rule lifetime the middlebox allows, and midcomConfigPersistentRules says whether rules can be stored persistently. A per-interface BITS object, midcomConfigIfBits, reports IPv4 and IPv6 support, address and port wildcards, firewall and NAT functionality, port translation, protocol translation, twice-NAT and whether the interface is an inside interface. Index 0 covers all interfaces. midcomConfigFirewallTable sets the group name and priority used for all MIDCOM firewall rules at an interface. These configuration objects are typically not meant to be written by MIDCOM clients.

Monitoring. midcomResourceTable links each policy rule to the NAT bindings, NAT sessions or firewall rule it uses, which can be correlated with the NAT-MIB (RFC 4008). Rules from different clients may share one NAT binding or firewall rule, so implementations must manage common properties such as lifetime carefully. The midcomStatistics subtree counts owners, rejected rules and reserve and enable rules that are active, expired or terminated.

Notifications. midcomUnsolicitedRuleEvent reports asynchronous changes to a rule, such as lifetime or idle time expiring. midcomSolicitedRuleEvent answers reserve, enable and rule lifetime change requests, and midcomSolicitedGroupEvent answers group lifetime changes.
sections.plainLanguage: There is a label saying what the box can do, a logbook of which doors each request opened, and a doorbell that rings when something changes.

sections.title: Recommendations for Operation
sections.content:
Command Responders implementing the MIB are RECOMMENDED to use the authPriv security level for all users, and to use VACM for the rule and group tables. Each client should only reach entries whose first index, midcomRuleOwner, matches its SNMP securityName or VACM groupName, for read, write and notify access. Exceptions include a standby MIDCOM agent for fail-over and a supervisor agent.

A notification target SHOULD be configured for each client, and clients SHOULD be able to start and stop their own notifications through snmpNotifyFilterTable. Two clients modifying the same rule should be avoided, for example by scheduling access, using different group indexes, or using non-overlapping rule index ranges.

Interface indexes from the IF-MIB may change after re-initialization, so clients must be aware that the interface a stored index points to may differ. Section 6.7 repeats that applications that cannot supply both private and public address information may not fit this MIB.
sections.plainLanguage: Each visitor should only be allowed to touch their own papers, and the lock should be a strong one.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Securing firewall and NAT configuration is extremely important. Compliant implementations MUST support SNMPv3 security services including data integrity, identity authentication, data confidentiality and replay protection, and deploying SNMP versions before SNMPv3 is NOT RECOMMENDED. Using USM and VACM is RECOMMENDED.

The most dangerous threat is unauthorized establishment of policy rules, which could open pinholes or create NAT bindings and so give access to protected networks, expose confidential information, allow attacks from outside, or stop a firewall blocking denial-of-service attacks. Implementations MUST provide strict authentication, message integrity checks and write access control for the rule and group tables. Write access to midcomRuleAdminStatus is particularly sensitive, because it causes rules to be established.

The RFC also discusses unauthorized reading of middlebox configuration and of the MIDCOM service configuration. The owner index is meant to make VACM views easy to set up, since midcomRuleOwner has the syntax of SnmpAdminString and maps onto a securityName or groupName.
sections.plainLanguage: Whoever can ask the firewall to open doors can let burglars in, so only trusted people with proven identity may ask.
